chunks: And as for what was narrated - Humayd ibn al-Ziyad from al-Hasan ibn Sama'ah from Sulayman ibn Dawud or some of our companions from him from Ali ibn Abi Hamzah from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:

I said: A man from your mawali died and left behind young children and left some property, and he had a debt, but the creditors did not know about it. If the debt is paid, his children will be left with nothing. He said: 'Spend it on his children.'

This is a continuous report, but there is doubt in its narration, so it is not permissible to deviate from the two preceding reports in favor of it, because the report of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj is well-attested and consistent with all the principles. This is because it is not valid that expenditure is made on the heirs from what they did not inherit, and they do not have an inheritance if there is a debt in any case.
Because Allah, the Exalted, said: 'After any bequest that is bequeathed or a debt.'
So it was stipulated that for the inheritance to be valid, it must be after the debt. And that which reveals this as well is what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: How is a deceased person's hidden debt handled regarding inheritance distribution in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi evaluates the reliability of a report where Imam al-Rida permits spending on young children from an estate with hidden debts, ultimately rejecting it as 'Maqtu' (disconnected) in favor of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj’s more robust narration. This preference aligns with the foundational Quranic principle that inheritance distribution is contingent upon the prior settlement of debts, ensuring the heirs' rights are not compromised by undisclosed liabilities.
